sections.b: Paul answers the question "Has God's word failed?" by pointing to how God has always chosen. Not all of Abraham's offspring are counted as his children: the line runs through Isaac, whom God promised (Romans 9:7-9). Rebecca's twins were told, before they were born and before they had done anything, "The elder will serve the younger" (Romans 9:12), so that God's purpose, which works by choosing, would stand "not by works but by the one who calls." Paul adds Malachi's "I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau" (Romans 9:13). The Old Testament passages he cites speak of nations (Genesis 25:23; Malachi 1:2-5), and Christians still differ on whether Paul has persons or peoples in mind. The cards on Romans 9 give each church's statement.

sections.h: Romans 9:14-24: mercy, Pharaoh and the potter
sections.b: When Paul asks, "Is God unjust?", he answers with Moses and Pharaoh. God's words in Exodus 33:19, spoken after the golden calf, are about his freedom to show mercy (Romans 9:15-16). Pharaoh is the example of a king whom God raised up to show his power (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). The potter's right over his clay (Romans 9:21; Isaiah 29:16; Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1-12) closes the answer, and the sentence about the vessels of anger and the vessels of mercy is left unfinished (Romans 9:22-24). Debated points: whether the vessels are fixed, whether "fitted for destruction" is passive or reflexive, and whether the vessels of mercy are Jews and Gentiles alike.
sections.refs: Romans 9:14-24; Exodus 33:19; Exodus 9:16; Isaiah 29:16; Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1-12

sections.h: Romans 11: an election of grace, and a people still loved
sections.b: In chapter 11 the word changes its object. The remnant "chosen by grace" (Romans 11:5) is a small group inside Israel, while "From the point of view of election, they are beloved, for the sake of the patriarchs" (Romans 11:28) is about all of Israel, the people. The same word eklogē covers both. Paul also says God "knew beforehand" his people (Romans 11:2) and that the "chosen" obtained what Israel was seeking, while the rest were hardened (Romans 11:7). Election in these chapters is first of all God's free, unearned love, and Paul ends the whole argument in praise of a mercy that has not finished (Romans 11:32-36).

common: In Romans 9 to 11 election is not earned by works or ancestry: it rests on God's call and mercy (Romans 9:11-12; 11:5-6).
uncommon: Paul's cases of Isaac, Jacob and Pharaoh speak only of roles in the history of God's people, and say nothing about anyone's final salvation.

claude.title: Three uses of "election" in Romans 9-11 (Claude's observation)
claude.body: Paul uses the same Greek family of words for three different objects in three chapters: God's purpose that works by choice (9:11), a remnant within Israel (11:5, 7), and Israel as a whole people (11:28). A reader who carries one meaning from one place to another, for example from the remnant of 11:5 to the beloved nation of 11:28, will find a contradiction that Paul does not feel. This is my own observation; it overlaps with the corporate readings of Dunn and Wright and with Barth's idea of one election with two forms.

sections.h: Romans 9: "Not all who are from Israel are Israel"
sections.b: Paul begins with Israel's gifts, which are still theirs: the adoption as children, the glory, the covenants, the lawgiving, the sacred service and the promises (Romans 9:4-5). Then he says that being born into Israel is not the same as being counted as Israel (Romans 9:6-8), and that God calls people "not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles" (Romans 9:24-26). The sentence is used in several ways: for a faithful remnant inside the nation, for the church as the true Israel, and for a people redefined by God's call. The card on Romans 9 gives the churches' positions.

The olive tree of Romans 11:16-24 has a root, natural branches and wild branches grafted in. The Gentile believer is warned not to boast: "you are not holding up the root. The root is holding you up" (Romans 11:18). The picture has only one tree. Readers differ on whether it means the church is Israel, with Gentiles joined to it, or that the church has taken Israel's place for the branches cut off, or that Jews and Gentiles share one people with different callings. Ephesians 2:11-22 speaks of Gentiles brought near, "citizens" with the saints, in a similar picture.

sections.h: Romans 11:25-29: all Israel and the irrevocable call
sections.b: Paul tells a mystery: a hardening has come upon part of Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, "and so all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25-26). He adds that "God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:29). Six main readings of "all Israel" are set out in the note on 11:26. The second sentence is the main text in Christian statements since 1965 that read Israel's calling as still standing (Nostra Aetate 4; John Paul II at Mainz in 1980, who spoke of the Old Covenant as never revoked; the Vatican commission's reflection of 2015, which says it is not a doctrinal text). The ELCA declaration of 1994 repudiated Luther's anti-Jewish writings. Earlier teaching often held that the church had replaced Israel (supersessionism); the deep dive on Romans 11 traces that history.

common: Most New Testament scholars hold that Romans 11 does not teach that God has cast Israel off in favor of the church, though they disagree about what it does teach; some Reformed and Catholic readers hold that the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared with the Gentiles (Romans 11:1-2, 17-18, 29).
uncommon: Romans 11:26 means that Jews are saved by God's covenant without faith in Jesus (the Sonderweg reading), a view held by a minority and disputed by most (see the note on Romans 11:26).

claude.title: The word "Israel" in Romans 9-11 (Claude's observation)
claude.body: Paul uses "Israel" in several ways: the whole people (9:4; 11:1), the faithful core (9:6; 11:7) and the people whom God will save (11:26). In Romans 9-11 he never calls the church "Israel," which is a reason for caution in using these chapters to say the church is the new Israel. He does call Gentile believers wild branches grafted into Israel's tree. This is my own reading; it overlaps with Nanos, Kinzer and Wright, although they do not all draw the same conclusion.
claude.refs: Romans 9:4; Romans 9:6; Romans 11:1; Romans 11:7; Romans 11:17; Romans 11:26

sections.b: Paul quotes Isaiah to show that the smallness of the believing part of Israel is nothing new: "Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand by the sea, only the remnant will be saved" (Romans 9:27, from Isaiah 10:22), and "Unless the Lord of Armies had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom" (Romans 9:29, from Isaiah 1:9). In Isaiah the remnant were the survivors of the Assyrian invasion (Isaiah 10:20-22; Isaiah 7:3). Paul reads it as God's faithfulness: a seed is left, and through it the promise lives.

sections.h: Romans 11:1-6: Elijah and the seven thousand
sections.b: To show that God has not rejected his people, Paul offers himself, an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1). He then recalls Elijah at Horeb, who thought he was alone, and God's answer, "I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal" (Romans 11:3-4; 1 Kings 19:10-18). The present remnant is "chosen by grace" (Romans 11:5), and the point of the Elijah story is that the remnant is God's own doing. For Paul the first members of this remnant are the Jewish believers in Jesus; the remnant is a pledge, not a final number (Romans 11:15-16).

common: Paul's "remnant" is the believing part of Israel in his own day, a sign that God has not cast off his people (Romans 11:1-5).
uncommon: The remnant of Romans 11:5 includes all elect Jews of every age, not only the first generation of believers.

claude.title: A remnant that is also a firstfruit (Claude's observation)
claude.body: Paul calls the remnant a remnant in 11:5 and then, a few verses later, uses the word "firstfruit" for something that makes the whole batch holy (11:16). That turns the idea from subtraction (what is left over) into promise (what is first). The two images together suggest that the remnant is not only a survivor but a guarantee. This is my own reading, which overlaps with commentators who see the firstfruit as the Jewish believers.

sections.h: Romans 9:17-18: Pharaoh and the freedom of mercy
sections.b: Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh, "For this very reason I raised you up: that in you I might show my power, and that my name might be told through all the earth" (Romans 9:17, from Exodus 9:16), and concludes: "he shows mercy to whom he wants, and he hardens whom he wants" (Romans 9:18). In Exodus the hardening has both a human and a divine subject: Pharaoh's heart "was stubborn" or he "made his heart heavy" (Exodus 7:13; 8:15, 32; 9:34), and the LORD "made Pharaoh's heart stubborn" (Exodus 9:12; 10:20, 27; 14:4, 8), after announcing it beforehand (Exodus 4:21; 7:3). Christians differ on how the two fit: God's act as cause, God's act as judgment on one who first hardened himself, or God's permission.
sections.refs: Romans 9:17-18; Exodus 4:21; Exodus 7:3; Exodus 8:15; Exodus 9:12; Exodus 9:16

sections.h: Romans 11:7-10 and 25: the hardening of part of Israel
sections.b: Paul says that "the rest were hardened" (Romans 11:7), using a different verb from 9:18, poroo, from a word for a callus. He weaves Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10 into one line, "God gave them a spirit of numbness" (Romans 11:8), and adds Psalm 69:22-23 (Romans 11:9-10), and he sets a limit: the hardening has come "upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in" (Romans 11:25). Israel's stumble is not a fall (Romans 11:11); the hardening serves a purpose, and it has an end. The Gospels use the same family of words of the disciples (Mark 6:52; 8:17) and of those who heard Jesus (John 12:40).
sections.refs: Romans 11:7-10; Romans 11:25; Deuteronomy 29:4; Isaiah 29:10; Psalm 69:22-23; Mark 6:52; John 12:40

common: In Exodus Pharaoh's hardening of himself comes first in the plague story, and God's hardening comes after (Exodus 7:13; 8:15; 9:12).
uncommon: God's hardening in Romans 9 is the only cause of Pharaoh's refusal, from before the first plague (Exodus 4:21; 7:3).

claude.title: Two words for hardening, two directions (Claude's observation)
claude.body: Paul's verb in 9:18 (sklerynei, "makes hard") is used of Pharaoh and ends in a verdict about God's freedom; his verb in 11:7 and 11:25 (poroo and porosis) is used of Israel and ends in a limit ("until"). The two uses sit on different sides of the chapter break and lead to different conclusions: mercy to whom he wishes, and a hardening that stops. This is my own observation, and it does not settle how the two should be related.

sections.h: Paul's conscience and his grief for Israel
sections.b: Paul opens chapters 9 to 11 with a near-oath: he tells the truth in Christ, he is not lying, and his conscience bears witness along with him in the Holy Spirit (Romans 9:1). He calls his own conscience as a witness to a feeling, his unceasing grief for Israel, that his readers in Rome might doubt. Here conscience is an inner witness that confirms what a person says, shared with the Spirit. The Greek word syneidesis means "knowing together with oneself."

When Paul lists what God gave Israel, the first item is "the adoption as children" (Romans 9:4). The nation was called God's firstborn son (Exodus 4:22) before believers were told they had received the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15, 23). So Israel's adoption comes first in the story, and the church's adoption shares in it rather than replacing it. Hosea's promise that those who are "not my people" will be called "sons of the living God" (Romans 9:26) widens the same adoption to the Gentiles.
